name: Promptmetheus
tagline: An IDE for writing, testing and comparing LLM prompts across many models, with cost and output tracking.

pricing.notes: AI-drafted from a site submission; price unverified.

verdictSummary: This is a workbench on top of other people's APIs, which is the easiest category of app to clone for one person. The actual loop is: compose a prompt from blocks, swap variables, fan the same prompt out across several models, see outputs side by side with token cost, rate them, keep the history. A coding agent can put that on your machine in an afternoon if you route everything through a single gateway instead of hand-writing six provider clients. What you cannot clone in a sitting is the polish: the keyboard-driven editing, the tidy stats, the shared team prompt library, the years of small decisions that make it feel like a tool rather than a form. If you are a solo builder who just wants a prompt lab with your own keys and no seat fee, the DIY version is genuinely fine.
coreLoopDIY: A local prompt workbench that composes prompts from reusable blocks with variables, runs them across several models in a matrix, and stores outputs, ratings and token cost in SQLite.
requirements: An OpenRouter API key (or one provider key) in .env
Local disk for the SQLite file
whatYouLose: Shared team workspaces and a collaborative prompt library
Curated, maintained coverage of dozens of providers and models as they churn
Polished stats, comparison views and prompt version history
Hosted access from any browser or device without you running anything
Someone else fixing it when a provider changes its API shape
moatNotes: The moat is ergonomics and breadth of model coverage, not data. Nothing about your prompts gets more valuable because other people use the same tool.
whyPeopleStillPay: Because prompt work is fiddly and a tool that already handles block composition, variable sets, multi-model fan-out, cost math and prompt history is worth more than the hours you would spend re-implementing them badly. Teams also pay for the shared library: one canonical place where the production prompts live, with history, instead of four people pasting into a chat window. And if you evaluate across many providers regularly, keeping current with model lists and parameter quirks is real unpaid maintenance work that a subscription quietly absorbs.
notes: Prompt tooling is the one category where the buyers are exactly the people most capable of building it themselves, which is why this space is crowded and cheap.
prompt:
Build a local prompt engineering workbench. Single user, runs on my machine, no accounts, no telemetry, no cloud services beyond the LLM API itself.

Stack, non negotiable: Next.js 15 with the App Router, TypeScript, Tailwind, SQLite via better-sqlite3 with a file at ./data/prompts.db. No ORM, plain SQL in a small db module. No auth. No Docker.

Model access: talk to OpenRouter's OpenAI-compatible chat completions endpoint only. Read OPENROUTER_API_KEY from .env.local and write a .env.example. Ship a hardcoded list of about eight model ids in a config file I can edit; do not try to fetch a live catalog.

Data model: Prompt (name, description), Block (belongs to a prompt, ordered, type of system or user or context, text with {{variable}} placeholders), VariableSet (named JSON key/value map per prompt), Run (prompt id, model id, resolved input, output text, prompt tokens, completion tokens, estimated cost, latency ms, rating 0-5, note, created at).

UI, three screens:
1. Prompt list: create, rename, delete, duplicate.
2. Prompt editor: add/edit/reorder/delete blocks in a left column, live resolved preview on the right, variable set editor below with a raw JSON textarea and a save-as-named-set button.
3. Run matrix: pick one or more models and one or more variable sets, hit Run, and execute every combination with a concurrency limit of 3. Show results in a grid of cards: output text, token counts, cost, latency, a 0-5 star control and a note field, both saved immediately.

Also: a history view per prompt, filterable by model and minimum rating, and a button to export all runs for a prompt as CSV.

Cost: put per-million input and output prices next to each model id in the same config file. Compute cost from returned usage. If usage is missing, store null and display a dash, do not guess.

Errors: if a call fails, save the run with the error string in the output field and mark it failed. One bad model must never kill the batch.

Out of scope, do not build: sharing, multi user, prompt chaining, evaluation scoring by another model, streaming responses, a settings UI for the API key.

Finish with a README that covers install, .env.local setup, npm run dev, and where to edit the model list.
